note: Ground truth derived from src/rules/the-one-rule.md as of 2026-10. Each item names the rule it probes and, where it has one, the TRAP — the specific misreading we expect. Scoring: a wrong answer is a comprehension failure; a right answer with a wrong derivation is luck and scores half; 'the pages do not say' is correct wherever stated.

items.q: A character with Firearms Score 17 shoots under conditions the GM rates as Ease Factor 4. What is the Success Chance, and what does the player roll?
items.a: SC = 17 x 4 = 68. Roll D100, succeeding on 68 or less.

items.q: A duellist has Melee Score 25. Her BEF is 5 and she is fighting at a range her weapon dislikes, worth -1. What is her Success Chance?
items.a: 100. A Score over 20 counts as 20 for the multiplication but adds +1 EF per 3 points above 20, so 25 is '20+1'. EF = 5 - 1 + 1 = 5. SC = 20 x 5 = 100.
items.trap: Multiplying 25 by the EF (giving 100 by a wrong route, or 125). The Score caps at 20; the surplus becomes EF, which is why the -1 is cancelled rather than paid.

items.q: Does a character with Score 22 roll any better than one with Score 20, all else equal?
items.a: No. The first bonus step is at 23 ('20+1 (23-25)'), so 21 and 22 count as 20 with no EF bonus.
items.probes: the granularity of the over-20 rule
items.trap: Assuming +1 EF per 3 points starts immediately at 21.

items.q: A task sits at Ease Factor 1 and the GM applies a -2 modifier. What is the resulting Ease Factor?
items.a: 1/4. The ladder is 0, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 3... so two steps left from 1 gives 1/2 then 1/4.
items.probes: the non-linear bottom of the ladder
items.trap: Arithmetic: 1 - 2 = -1, then clamping to 0. The ladder is positional, not numeric.

items.q: A task is at EF 6. Modifiers of +10 and -4 apply. What is the final Ease Factor?
items.a: 12. Sum the modifiers first (+6), then move six steps: 6 to 12. Applying them in sequence would cap at 15 and come back to 11.
items.trap: Applying modifiers one at a time, hitting the 15 ceiling, and losing the surplus.

items.q: A character with Score 13 attempts something at Ease Factor 1/4. What do they need to roll?
items.a: 3 or less. 13 x 1/4 = 3.25, and fractions round to nearest (1/2 or more rounds up).

items.q: Success Chance is 68. The player rolls 34. What Quality Rating is that?
items.a: QR3. The thresholds are SC/10 = 6.8, SC/4 = 17, SC/2 = 34, SC = 68; 34 is within SC/2, so QR3.
items.probes: reading the QR off one roll
items.trap: Off-by-one at the boundary: 34 is <= SC/2, so it is QR3 and not QR4.

items.q: Success Chance is 68. The player rolls 70. What happens?
items.a: QR10, a fumble: it went wrong. 70 is over the SC and a multiple of 10, which is the fumble condition.
items.trap: Reporting a plain failure (QR7) and missing that the roll is a multiple of 10.

items.q: A master has a Success Chance over 100. The player rolls 100. What is the result?
items.a: QR7, a plain failure — and the reviewer should flag that the page does not say so outright. The reasoning both blind runs found independently, and it is better than this bank's first answer: the QR10 row's condition is 'roll > SC', and if SC exceeds 100 then a roll of 100 is NOT over the SC, so the fumble row cannot fire by its own wording. 'Never better than QR7' is a ceiling and not a floor, so it does not exclude QR10 either. QR7 is the better reading; the text leaves it open.
items.probes: interaction of the two hard limits with the fumble rule
items.trap: Answering confidently either way. Credit QR7 with the '> SC is not met' reasoning; credit QR10 only if the reviewer notes the conflict. Penalise an unhedged answer.
items.note: Ground truth corrected 2026-10-08 after two independent blind runs gave a cleaner derivation than the one written here.

items.q: A weapon with Damage Class 8 hits at QR3. How much damage does it do?
items.a: 2. QR3 yields 50%, and Damage = Yield x DC / 2, so 0.5 x 8 / 2 = 2.
items.probes: the Yield column and the damage formula

items.q: Two different chaining rules appear on this page. A diagnosis rolled at QR2 feeds a repair; and separately, a prior result 'builds' into a following task at QR2. What modifier does each give, and why are they different?
items.a: The diagnosis gives PM = 4 - QR = +2. The build gives +(5 - QR) = +3. The page states both and does not reconcile them. A reviewer who reports this as an inconsistency, or asks which applies when, has found the real thing: these are deliberately separate (PM is the quality of a thing made, Build is momentum carried forward) but the page does not say so.
items.probes: whether two chaining formulas one page apart read as one rule misremembered
items.trap: This item has no clean answer by design. The finding is the point.

items.q: A player calls a head shot, accepting a penalty, and the roll succeeds. Does the GM now roll to see where the bullet landed?
items.a: No. 'Never penalize the same choice twice': the penalty was the price, so success means it landed where aimed. Pay once, up front.

items.q: An attacker and a defender both roll QR3. What happens?
items.a: Nothing decisive: equal QRs cancel. The blow is just parried and the struggle continues. If someone must act now, the higher Score edges it.
items.probes: opposed resolution and the deliberate stalemate
items.trap: Inventing a tiebreak (re-roll, higher roll wins) when the page states ties cancel.

items.q: A character fails to pick a lock. Can they simply try again until they succeed?
items.a: They can retry, but it is not free: a failure already spent the time (a QR7 eats about 200% of the estimate), so when time matters the guard is coming. A QR10 shuts the door entirely and they must find another way.
items.probes: why no explicit retry rule is needed
items.trap: Looking for a retry penalty or an attempt limit, which the page deliberately does not have.

items.q: The GM needs a Quality Rating for an unseen NPC's work, with no Score to roll against. What do they do?
items.a: Roll D10: 1 is QR1, 2 is QR2, 3-5 is QR3, 6-10 is QR4.

items.q: A penalty applies equally to an expert and an amateur attempting the same opposed task. Who is hurt more, and why?
items.a: The amateur. A shared penalty comes out of the amateur's chance of succeeding at all, but merely out of the expert's surplus. This is also why stacking several small ease-factor advantages beats holding out for one big one.
items.probes: whether the page's central claim about relative net success is legible
